newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-ORANGE SEES PRE-TAX PROFIT H1 '99.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-ORANGE SEES PRE-TAX PROFIT H1 '99.

text.p: British digital mobile telephone company Orange Plc said on Thursday it was on track to break into the black on a pre-tax level in the first half of 1999.

Finance director Graham Howe, who promised that Orange was "poised to set the agenda for the wirefree future" helped by planned new services, said the company was on course for a pre-tax profit on a month-on-month basis in the latter part of this year.
"If we turn in a profit latter part of next year it (a pre-tax profit) will be in the next reporting period after that," he told Reuters in an interview.

Helped by a growth in both its customer base and a 13 percent rise in annual revenues from each subscriber to 500 pounds, Orange earlier broke into the black for the first time on an EBIDTA level in the half year.
It reported earnings before interest, depreciation, tax and amortisation of 12 million pounds. Pre-tax losses narrowed by 41 percent to 74 million pounds.
The group, Britain's youngest mobile telephone company which has won 13.3 percent of the UK market, has built up its reputation and customer base on the back of an aggressive marketing campaign.
It is developing advanced new services such as Internet browsing, virtual banking and video telephony, the company said.
Orange said it would use up the headroom in a 1.2 billion pound debt facility, taken out 1995, to double to 800 million stg network investments by the end of 1999.
"That will provide a depth and quality of coverage not yet seen in the UK market," Howe said.
Orange will be looking soon to refinance the debt facility.
The group wants to take on the fixed-line operators.
Its customer base, now at one million customers, grew by 200,000 is the first half of the year and growth is traditionally higher in the second half of the year.
It says it envisages a future in which almost the entire British adult population will communicate at some point through a mobile device, believing industry estimates to be too conservative.
Analysts reckon mobile penetration in Britain, currently at around 13 percent, will rise to Scandinavian-type levels of 30 percent by 2006.

Orange also brushes aside some analyst suggestions that prices will have to fall dramatically to achieve those levels. Howe insisted that prices were competitive and said new connections of subscribers were as high as ever.

Orange, which has sealed roaming agreements across Europe and beyond, boasts that it has the most loyal customers of Britain's four mobile telephone operators. Its total churn rate -- the rate at which customers swap operators or are cut off -- came in at around 19.9 percent compared to an industry average of 30 percent.
The two biggest mobile telephone companies -- Vodafone Group Plc and Cellnet -- have a higher churn rate mainly because they are still taking customers from their analogue networks onto digital ones.
Having won a licence as part of a consortium to operate digital services in Austria, analysts expect Orange to look at similar opportunities in the Netherlands and Belgium.
